chunks: "The continuity condition for an inductor is that the current through it can't change instantaneously.
The current just after a switching event equals the current just before: i L(0^ plus ) equals i L(0^-) . So inductors resist changes in current.
The reason is the inductor equation, v equals L di over dt . If the current jumped, di/dt would be infinite, which needs infinite voltage.
You can also see it from energy: the inductor stores 1 over 2 LI squared , and changing that in zero time would need infinite power.
Notice the voltage across an inductor can jump; it's only the current that's continuous. Capacitors are the dual: their voltage is continuous.
That's how I start any switching transient.
At the instant after the switch moves, I replace the inductor with a current source equal to whatever it was carrying, and solve the circuit.
The practical consequence is inductive kick.

If an inductor is carrying current and you open a switch, the inductor will raise its voltage as high as it needs to keep that current flowing, even if it means arcing across the switch or avalanching a MOSFET.
That's why relay coils get a flyback diode across them: it gives the current somewhere to go so it can decay gracefully."
